power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A priori power analyses (G*Power 3.1; Faul et al., 2009), indicated that detecting medium effects (d = .50, α = .05, two-tailed mean comparisons) with 80% power required 64 participants per group. Previous research evaluating a digital parenting intervention identified such a medium effect on parenting for the interaction term between an intervention and control group (d = .51, Yap et al., 2019). A meta-analysis on online parenting programs found large effects on positive parenting (e.g., d = 1.00; Spencer et al., 2020). Hence, we expected medium effects on need-supportive parenting.

Previous research evaluating a digital parenting intervention identified such a medium effect on parenting for the interaction term between an intervention and control group (d = .51, Yap et al., 2019). A meta-analysis on online parenting programs found large effects on positive parenting (e.g., d = 1.00; Spencer et al., 2020). Hence, we expected medium effects on need-supportive parenting."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p-values >.063", "p-values >.807", "p-values > .087", "p-values > .106"), Sentence = c("Group comparisons (Table 3) identified no significant differences between intervention groups (pooled) and controls (H1) (-.04 < d < .13; p-values >.063).", "Furthermore, no group differences were found between the personalized and universal intervention groups (H2) (-.01 < d < .02; p-values >.807) in parent-reported parenting.", "Comparing controls with the pooled intervention groups yielded no group differences for changes in positive affect, negative affect or stress (-.11 < d < .09; p-values > .087, Table 3).", "The personalized intervention group compared to the universal intervention group did not show different changes in positive affect, negative affect or stress (-.11 < d < .17; p-values > .106), rejecting H4." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Ethics Approval.
Ethical approval was obtained by the Research Ethics Review Committee of the Erasmus University Rotterdam (ETH2324-0930) on the 28 th of August, 2024.
The study was conducted in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Consent to Participate.
All participants provided digital active informed consent before participation in the study.
For adolescents under 16 years of age, all legal guardians provided consent for their child's participation.
Adolescent mental health problems, such as depressive symptoms and anxiety, are rising globally (e.g., McGorry et al., 2024; Inchley et al. 2020).
text.formatted: Adolescent mental health problems, such as depressive symptoms and anxiety, are rising globally (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">McGorry et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Inchley et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Strengthening parenting might be an underexplored target for preventing adolescent mental health problems (Morris et al., 2021; Restifo & Bögels, 2009).
text.formatted: Strengthening parenting might be an underexplored target for preventing adolescent mental health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Morris et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Restifo & Bögels, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Theoretical work (e.g., Soenens et al., 2017; 2019) proposes that parenting strategies such as nurturing a positive relationship (hereafter: support), considering adolescents' perspective and providing choice (i.e. autonomy support), and establishing clear expectations and consequences (i.e., structure) are vital to adolescents' mental well-being.
text.formatted: Theoretical work (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Soenens et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019)</ref> proposes that parenting strategies such as nurturing a positive relationship (hereafter: support), considering adolescents' perspective and providing choice (i.e. autonomy support), and establishing clear expectations and consequences (i.e., structure) are vital to adolescents' mental well-being.

text.text: However, few parenting interventions translate these insights into accessible, evidence-based programs (David et al., 2023; Spencer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, few parenting interventions translate these insights into accessible, evidence-based programs <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(David et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Spencer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, this study developed and tested a new "PARADOx" digital parenting intervention that aims to strengthen need-supportive parenting practices, improving adolescent mental well-being.
Many parenting resources offer advice on parenting adolescents, ranging from books, to professional advice, to smartphone applications.
Digital interventions are highly scalable and cost-effective compared to offline interventions (Gentili et al., 2022), making them particularly suited to prevention.
text.formatted: Digital interventions are highly scalable and cost-effective compared to offline interventions <ref type="bibr">(Gentili et al., 2022)</ref>, making them particularly suited to prevention.

text.text: However, evidence-based preventive parenting programs in the context of promoting adolescent mental health remain rare (Yap et al., 2016).
text.formatted: However, evidence-based preventive parenting programs in the context of promoting adolescent mental health remain rare <ref type="bibr">(Yap et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We are aware of few such programs.

First, recent meta-analyses of online parenting interventions (David et al., 2023; Spencer et al., 2020) identified a web-based parenting intervention specifically for adolescent mental health: Partners in Parenting (PiP; Yap et al., 2017).
text.formatted: First, recent meta-analyses of online parenting interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(David et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Spencer et al., 2020)</ref> identified a web-based parenting intervention specifically for adolescent mental health: Partners in Parenting (PiP; <ref type="bibr">Yap et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: PiP showed promising short-and medium-term effects on parenting practices such as establishing rules and consequences (Yap et al., 2018; 2019).
text.formatted: PiP showed promising short-and medium-term effects on parenting practices such as establishing rules and consequences <ref type="bibr">(Yap et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, adolescents' mental health problems did not significantly decrease compared to controls at 12-month follow-up, and parent-reports did not translate to adolescent perceptions of parenting (Yap et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, adolescents' mental health problems did not significantly decrease compared to controls at 12-month follow-up, and parent-reports did not translate to adolescent perceptions of parenting <ref type="bibr">(Yap et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Second, one recently developed digital intervention successfully improved autonomysupportive practices in mothers whose children were transitioning to secondary school (Duchesne et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, one recently developed digital intervention successfully improved autonomysupportive practices in mothers whose children were transitioning to secondary school <ref type="bibr">(Duchesne et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, child mental well-being was not assessed.
Both interventions highlight the potential of accessible digital tools to strengthen parenting during adolescence, yet either did not assess or find an impact on adolescent mental well-being.

Inspired by developments (Ramchandani et al., 2023) in domains where digital interventions are upcoming and widely used in treating and preventing adolescent mental health problems (Dietvorst et al., 2024) and personalizing medicine and therapy (Ng & Weisz, 2015), we developed a digital parenting intervention embedded within a 100-day diary study.
text.formatted: Inspired by developments <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Ramchandani et al., 2023)</ref> in domains where digital interventions are upcoming and widely used in treating and preventing adolescent mental health problems <ref type="bibr">(Dietvorst et al., 2024)</ref> and personalizing medicine and therapy <ref type="bibr">(Ng & Weisz, 2015)</ref>, we developed a digital parenting intervention embedded within a 100-day diary study.

text.text: The intervention includes two key-components beyond daily self-monitoring of parenting and well-being.
First, parents gained self-insight into parenting practices through a data-driven feedback report delivered on day 47.
Subsequently, in a 6-week advice phase between days 50 and 89, parents received brief parenting tips to enhance need-supportive parenting (structure, autonomy support and support) in daily life.

Our intervention was developed through an iterative process described in the https://osf.io/zfcmd/?view_only=d33029036c154278910d030b76c30281 Initial tips were constructed based on theory and focus groups with adolescents and parents, further curated through expert and parent ratings.
text.formatted: Our intervention was developed through an iterative process described in the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/zfcmd/?view_only=d33029036c154278910d030b76c30281">preregistered codebook:</ref> Initial tips were constructed based on theory and focus groups with adolescents and parents, further curated through expert and parent ratings.

text.text: Moreover, we developed two versions of the intervention: a universal version containing a feedback report with insights into daily parenting practices in an average family and expert-selected tips , and a personalized version consisting of a data-driven feedback report on families' own functioning and a choice between multiple tips.
Personalization of content is hypothesized to enhance relevance and effectiveness (August & Gewirtz, 2019; Ng & Weisz, 2015).
text.formatted: Personalization of content is hypothesized to enhance relevance and effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(August & Gewirtz, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ng & Weisz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Theory (e.g., Smith & Thelen, 2003) and empirical research suggest that parenting effects vary greatly across families (Boele et al., 2023; Bülow et al., 2022a).
text.formatted: Theory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Smith & Thelen, 2003)</ref> and empirical research suggest that parenting effects vary greatly across families <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Boele et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bülow et al., 2022a)</ref>.

text.text: However, we have encountered few parenting interventions tailored to individual families' dynamics and needs.
This randomized controlled trial (RCT) examined whether the PARADOx digital parenting intervention improved parenting practices (proximal outcome) and adolescent wellbeing (distal outcome).
Moreover, we explored if the intervention might unintentionally increase overprotection.

Overprotection refers to overly controlling and involved parenting (Ryan et al., 2024), which may frustrate adolescents' basis psychological needs and is associated with poorer mental health (e.g., anxiety; de Roo et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Overprotection refers to overly controlling and involved parenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Ryan et al., 2024)</ref>, which may frustrate adolescents' basis psychological needs and is associated with poorer mental health (e.g., anxiety; de <ref type="bibr">Roo et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Because overprotection often stems from good intentions (Segrin et al., 2012) we test whether our intervention risked parents overcorrecting and adopting "too much of a good thing."
text.formatted: Because overprotection often stems from good intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Segrin et al., 2012)</ref> we test whether our intervention risked parents overcorrecting and adopting "too much of a good thing."

text.text: We considered the intervention successful if need-supportive parenting increased without turning into overprotection, and adolescent's well-being improved.

We followed 547 adolescents and 541 parents with 100 daily diaries to test four preregistered hypotheses: • H1: Parents in intervention groups (universal or personalized) show greater increases in need-supportive parenting (structure, autonomy support, and support) than controls.
• H2: Personalized group parents show stronger increases in these parenting practices than parents in the universal group.
• H3: Adolescents in intervention groups show greater improvements in affective wellbeing (increased positive affect, decreased negative affect) than controls.
• H4: Adolescents whose parents received the personalized intervention show stronger gains in well-being than those in the universal group.

From October 21 st , participants received 111 Experience Sampling (ESM; Keijsers et al., 2022) surveys (5-6 times daily, ca. 2 minutes) and 100 daily surveys (ca. 3-5 minutes) on parenting practices and well-being.

text.text: ESM and daily surveys, including intervention parenting tips, were distributed via Avicenna.

Incentives aimed to promote participants' engagement (https://osf.io/zfcmd/?view_only=d33029036c154278910d030b76c30281), through enjoyment, self-insight and awareness of scientific impact (Bülow, Janssen et al., 2025).

text.text: Financial incentives were up to €105 for adolescents and €55 for parents, conditional upon engagement.
Adolescents could also win €25 gift cards.
Randomization was conducted in two phases.
First, via schools participants were recruited exclusively to the control or intervention group to minimize cross-group knowledge.
Recruitment per school was based on practical considerations (e.g., progress of participant enrollment).
Subsequently, all parents recruited to the intervention group were assigned to a universal or personalized intervention using an unstratified, unblocked simple randomization procedure via R-script.
Participants were not informed of different study conditions and were thus presumed blinded.
Recruitment procedures were identical across conditions but researchers were aware for which group they were recruiting.

While the control group engaged only in 100 days of self-monitoring via daily diaries, intervention groups received a universal or personalized version of two additional components (Figure 1): (1) a one-time parenting feedback report via E-mail based on selfmonitoring data and (2) brief parenting tips via the daily diaries three times per week for six weeks.

text.text: Participants were 547 adolescents aged 12-17 years (M = 14.1, SD = 1.6), and 541 parents (Mage = 46.7, SD = 4.7, range 31 to 61 years).
Participating parents were biological mothers (81%) or fathers (17%), n = 3 adoptive mothers, n = 1 stepmother, and n = 1 stepfather.
Parents were born in the Netherlands (92%), other European countries (4%), South America (1%), Africa (1%), Asia (1%) or North America (n = 1).
Most parents had completed a theoretical (college or university degree; 77%) or applied educational track (vocational training; 19%, High school; 4%).
Half (50%) of parents lived in an urban setting, 50% rural.

Most parents considered themselves the primary caregiver (33%) or shared parenting tasks equally (67%), n = 3 parents considered their role as parent "small", and most were together with the (other) biological parent (79%).
Among adolescents, 53% were girls, 46% boys, n = 1 non-binary.
Most adolescents (96%) were born in the Netherlands, or other European countries (2%).
Adolescents had one (53%), two (28%) or three (9%) siblings, 9% had no siblings.

Regarding education, 43% of adolescents followed a theoretical track (pre-university secondary education), 37% an applied track (higher general secondary education or college), 19% a practical track (pre-vocational secondary education or vocational training), and 3% a mixed track.
Participant attrition was low (Figure 2).

text.text: From baseline to post-intervention, adolescents reported a decrease in positive affect and increase in negative affect, but no notable changes in stress (Table 2, Figure 4).

text.text: Examining changes during the intervention showed that only adolescents in the universal intervention group demonstrated a decrease in positive affect and increase in negative affect, but not stress.

We assessed whether adolescents in both intervention groups (pooled) would report greater increases in affective well-being than controls (H3) and whether the personalized intervention group would improve more strongly than the universal intervention group (H4).
These hypothesis were not supported.
Comparing controls with the pooled intervention groups yielded no group differences for changes in positive affect, negative affect or stress (-.11 < d < .09; p-values > .087, Table 3).

text.text: The personalized intervention group compared to the universal intervention group did not show different changes in positive affect, negative affect or stress (-.11 < d < .17; p-values > .106), rejecting H4.

text.text: Additional analyses revealed that positive affect decreased more strongly only among adolescents in the universal intervention group compared to the control group (Est = -3.09, 95% CI [-5.46; -.72], p = .011).
To better understand these unexpected decreases in affective well-being, we explored well-being at the item level (Online Resource 1, Tables S7.1 and S7.2).

Parents are vital to adolescent well-being (e.g. Soenens et al., 2017; 2019) but digital evidence-based parenting programs for supporting adolescent well-being remain scarce (David et al., 2023; Spencer et al., 2020).

text.text: This preregistered RCT investigated short-term effects of our novel PARADOx digital parenting intervention, encompassing a data-driven feedback report based on daily self-monitoring, and parenting tips.
On average across the sample, parents became more critical of their parenting, but adolescents appraised the needsupportiveness of their parents increasingly positive.
The harmful practice of overprotection declined according to parents and adolescents.
However, the main hypotheses that datadriven feedback reports and parenting tips (personalized or universal) would have benefits above and beyond self-monitoring were not supported.
These findings and their implications are discussed below.

Online parenting programs to promote adolescent well-being are generally more accessible and scalable than traditional, offline interventions (Gentili et al., 2022) and can facilitate personalization (August & Gewirtz, 2019), but remain rare (e.g. David et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Online parenting programs to promote adolescent well-being are generally more accessible and scalable than traditional, offline interventions <ref type="bibr">(Gentili et al., 2022)</ref> and can facilitate personalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(August & Gewirtz, 2019)</ref>, but remain rare (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">David et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research demonstrated the feasibility of self-monitoring daily family processes among 15 families (Swendeman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous research demonstrated the feasibility of self-monitoring daily family processes among 15 families <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Swendeman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Following more than 500 families for 100 days, we demonstrate its applicability at a larger scale.
Moreover, parents in intervention groups displayed higher engagement than controls, suggesting a motivational element of learning about yourself, and your family system (Bülow, et al, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, parents in intervention groups displayed higher engagement than controls, suggesting a motivational element of learning about yourself, and your family system <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bülow, et al, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, mass prevention programs for parents can be tailored via data-driven approaches with theory guided advice.

We hypothesized that families receiving the intervention would display stronger improvements in need-supportive parenting (H1) and adolescent well-being (H3) than controls who only monitored their (family) functioning.
However, no group differences were detected.
Effects of our feedback report and parenting tips beyond self-monitoring may have been too small to detect for several reasons.
First, given the complex, dynamic nature of parenting, interventions may require time to compound into genuine change in parenting, and especially to affect adolescent well-being.
Indeed, effects on parenting may appear months after a parenting intervention ended (e.g., Yap et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Indeed, effects on parenting may appear months after a parenting intervention ended (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Yap et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Second, because tips were embedded in the daily diaries, their availability was limited and their application depended on parents' engagement.
Third, mean levels of parenting practices, particularly autonomy support, were high.
Some participants may have felt little need to engage in a parenting intervention, which is supported by the finding that mainly structure improved (the lowest scoring practice).
Future research may help determine for which families this intervention may be (most) effective, for instance those with lower levels of need-supportive parenting.
Contrary to our hypotheses, the personalized intervention did not outperform the universal intervention in strengthening need-supportive parenting (H2) or adolescent affect (H4).

However, adolescents in the universal intervention group, but not the personalized intervention, decreased in positive affect and increased in negative affect, reflecting a potential detrimental side-effect of the universal intervention.
Exploring potential harms and their mechanisms could be of importance to intervention research (O'Donohue, 2026), especially given the scalability of digital parenting interventions.
Personalization may explain why adolescent affective well-being decreased specifically for the universal intervention.
Across interventions, parents were asked to apply tips they felt matched their family's needs.
Misaligned advice may frustrate adolescents' psychological needs, reducing affective wellbeing (Rodríguez-Meirinhos et al., 2020).
Personalization potentially promoted parents' sense of autonomy and competence to apply tips they felt matched their family, and decline tips which did not.
Parents in the personalized intervention could choose between multiple tips.
Choice can promote intrinsic motivation, effort, performance, and sense of competence (Patall et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Choice can promote intrinsic motivation, effort, performance, and sense of competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Patall et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The personalized feedback report may have further aided parents' sense of agency and competence in selecting tips by providing insight into their own family dynamics.

Conversely, in the universal intervention the report on average parenting practices and no choice between tips may have felt more normative and limited parents' sense of autonomy in applying or declining tips.

Hence, parents in the universal intervention may have felt pressured to implement tips they thought did not (optimally) match them or their child, potentially frustrating their child's needs and harming affective well-being.
Therefore, we tentatively suggest that personalization may still be an important intervention component for averting harmful side-effects.
Future research might determine if, and which aspects of personalization are most salient for averting harms, for whom, why, and when.Parents

An unexpected finding of the study is that across the sample, parents generally became more critical of their parenting (i.e., decreased autonomy support and support) whereas adolescents appraised their parents more positively (i.e., increased parental support and structure).
Adolescents reporting more parental support than parents themselves is not unexpected (Mastrotheodoros et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Adolescents reporting more parental support than parents themselves is not unexpected <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Mastrotheodoros et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Potentially, these findings reflect increased parental awareness rather than deteriorations in need-supportive parenting.

Earlier work suggests that daily reflection makes parents more aware of their parenting, including perceived shortcomings, but could make adolescents more appreciative of their parents (Swendeman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Earlier work suggests that daily reflection makes parents more aware of their parenting, including perceived shortcomings, but could make adolescents more appreciative of their parents <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Swendeman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In essence, adolescents' perceptions of their parents as need-supportive may be more essential to their well-being than parents' actual behavior (Soenens et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In essence, adolescents' perceptions of their parents as need-supportive may be more essential to their well-being than parents' actual behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Soenens et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, item-specific analyses suggest that adolescents increasingly approached their parents as confidants and sources of support, suggesting children's agency in shaping parental support in general (Šutić et al., 2025 (Šutić et al., , Boele et al., 2023) ) and in intervention settings (Novick et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Accordingly, item-specific analyses suggest that adolescents increasingly approached their parents as confidants and sources of support, suggesting children's agency in shaping parental support in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Šutić et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Šutić et al., , Boele et al., 2023) )</ref> and in intervention settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Novick et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This may reflect changes in parenting, or adolescents' increased awareness of their needs or their parents' availability due to their own reflections.
Simultaneously, only parents in the control group reported further decreases in autonomy support and support in the intervention phase.
This tentatively suggests that the intervention halted an overly critical appraisal of parenting.
Therefore, we suggest that feedback might still be important in addition to self-monitoring to increase parental confidence.

Overprotection is characterized by overly controlling and involved parenting (e.g., Ryan et al., 2024) and associated with adolescent mental health problems such as symptoms of depression and anxiety (e.g. de Roo et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Overprotection is characterized by overly controlling and involved parenting (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ryan et al., 2024)</ref> and associated with adolescent mental health problems such as symptoms of depression and anxiety (e.g. de Roo et al., 2020).

text.text: One potential risk of parenting advice we had anticipated, is parents becoming overly involved.

Observational data suggest the opposite: parents and adolescents reported a significant decrease in overprotection from baseline to post-intervention, suggesting that daily reflection and parenting advice might reduce this harmful practice.
This three-arm RCT, incorporating parent and adolescent reports, allowed us to assess a new digital parenting intervention, and compare universal and lightly personalized intervention formats.
However, some limitations warrant mention.

First, allocation of schools to recruitment for the control or intervention condition was not fully random but influenced by success of recruitment, potentially introducing some influence of school-level characteristics on recruitment between study conditions.
However, we found no baseline differences between groups where we found significant change.
Additionally, our measure of structure correlated poorly for parent-reports.
Future research might investigate differences in how parents apply the expression of expectations and confidence.
Second, personalization was light.
Parents received insight into their own family dynamics, but advice was not tailored to family dynamics, instead relying on parents' expertise for choosing tips.
Future studies might explore the effect of true personalization of content, for instance based on personal learning objectives.
Third, compared to programs which found medium-sized effects (e.g., Yap et al., 2019), dosage of our advice was small.
From a dynamic systems perspective, such light advice may be insufficient to change stable, rooted habits (Verplanken & Orbell, 2022).
text.formatted: From a dynamic systems perspective, such light advice may be insufficient to change stable, rooted habits <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Verplanken & Orbell, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, dosage was in line with light digital lifestyle interventions in other domains which demonstrated potential for behavior change (Dao et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, dosage was in line with light digital lifestyle interventions in other domains which demonstrated potential for behavior change <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dao et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Future research might investigate the optimal dosage of advice, specifically within the parenting domain.
Despite the large sample size (Spencer et al., 2020), this study may have been underpowered to find intervention effects smaller than in related studies (e.g., Yap et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Despite the large sample size <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Spencer et al., 2020)</ref>, this study may have been underpowered to find intervention effects smaller than in related studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Yap et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This is supported by slightly positive but non-significant trends in for example parentreported structure and autonomy support in intervention groups compared to controls.
Potentially, our control group, which monitored parenting and well-being daily, may have been too active to find the expected effects.

A recent meta-analysis on digital parenting interventions highlighted that RCT's with an active control group demonstrated notably smaller effects on parents and children compared to wait-list controls (David et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis on digital parenting interventions highlighted that RCT's with an active control group demonstrated notably smaller effects on parents and children compared to wait-list controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(David et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, due to the quantity of analyses run, which risks Type I errors, exploratory findings should be carefully interpreted and replicated in future studies.
Finally, despite recruitment targeting a diverse sample, the majority of our parents were highly educated, limiting generalizability to other families.

This study tested a novel digital parenting intervention, "PARADOx" to promote adolescent well-being among 500 parent-adolescent dyads, combining self-monitoring through 100 daily diaries, data-driven feedback, and tips on need-supportive parenting.
According to adolescents, parents generally became more need-supportive (increased parental support and structure).

text.text: Recruitment occurred through parent information evenings, class visits, newsletters, and flyers, as well as through previous study participants who consented to future contact, and adolescent peer referral.
Parents had to live with their participating child at least three days per week, speak Dutch, and own a smartphone (Android or iPhone) compatible with the data-collection app Avicenna.
No explicit exclusion criteria were specified.
Interested participants received an information letter and could contact researchers for questions.
Participants registered through an online informed consent form which included eligibility screening and assistance with installing the Avicenna application.
All participants provided active consent.
For adolescents under 16, both parents provided consent.
Recruitment materials are available in the preregistered codebook.
